details:
Orbit Craft — Space Mission Design Game

Orbit Craft is an interactive, browser-based space mission design game developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It allows players to experience the process of planning and designing a space mission by making engineering decisions, managing limited resources, and testing whether their mission can successfully meet its scientific objectives.

Players begin by selecting one of four real-world NASA mission references: Landsat 9 (Earth observation), Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (lunar science), GOES-R Series (weather monitoring), or Parker Solar Probe (solar science).

After selecting a mission, players configure its architecture by choosing a launch vehicle, spacecraft bus, power system, communication equipment, scientific instruments, ground stations, and data-access options. Each decision affects important mission constraints, including mass, power consumption, budget, data generation, communication capacity, and operational lifetime.

The game evaluates these decisions through engineering checks and a six-stage mission simulation. Players can see whether their spacecraft satisfies its requirements, identify design problems, and understand how different engineering choices influence mission success. The project also incorporates basic orbital mechanics, including Kepler's third law, to introduce players to orbital-period calculations.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Space exploration involves complex engineering decisions, but understanding these decisions should not require an advanced aerospace engineering background. Orbit Craft makes these concepts more approachable through interactive learning and experimentation.

Its intended benefits include:

  • Introducing students and beginners to spacecraft design and mission planning.
  • Demonstrating the relationships between spacecraft mass, power, communications, budgets, and scientific objectives.
  • Encouraging critical thinking, engineering problem-solving, and resource management.
  • Making space science and mission architecture more engaging through hands-on experimentation.
  • Helping users understand how real scientific missions are planned and why engineering constraints matter.

Our goal is to make the science and engineering behind space exploration accessible, engaging, and educational.

Tools and Technologies

Orbit Craft was developed as a browser-based application using:

  • HTML5 for the application structure.
  • CSS3 for the interface, responsive layouts, and visual design.
  • JavaScript for mission configuration, engineering calculations, validation, and simulation logic.
  • JSON for organizing mission references, spacecraft specifications, hardware catalogues, and other structured data.
  • NASA and JPL resources for scientific references, mission information, orbital mechanics concepts, and engineering context.
  • Git and GitHub for version control, project hosting, and deployment through GitHub Pages.

The application does not require specialized hardware or software installation; users can access it through a modern web browser.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of Orbit Craft lies in bringing multiple aspects of space mission engineering together into one interactive experience.

Instead of simply presenting information about rockets or spacecraft, the project allows players to make interconnected design decisions and immediately see their consequences. A heavier spacecraft may exceed a launch vehicle's payload capacity; a power-hungry instrument may require a more capable power system; and a high data-generation rate may require better communication infrastructure.

The four mission options also introduce different scientific objectives and operating environments, encouraging players to think beyond a single spacecraft design.

We incorporated orbital-period calculations based on Kepler's third law and an explanation of Earth-to-Moon transfers to connect the game with established orbital mechanics concepts.

Factors Considered During Development

Several factors guided our design:

  • Scientific relevance: Using real mission references and documented hardware specifications wherever available.
  • Engineering constraints: Making mass, power, cost, lifetime, and data requirements meaningful parts of mission design.
  • Educational accessibility: Keeping the interface understandable for users without an aerospace engineering background.
  • Mission diversity: Representing Earth observation, lunar science, weather monitoring, and solar science.
  • Technical accessibility: Developing a lightweight web application that does not require installation.
  • Scientific transparency: Distinguishing documented reference specifications from representative estimates and game-level calculations where exact data is unavailable.

Ultimately, Orbit Craft aims to turn the complexity of space mission planning into an accessible, interactive learning experience where players can explore, experiment, make mistakes, and understand what it takes to design a successful space mission.

AI USAGE

Generative AI tools, specifically Claude by Anthropic and ChatGPT by OpenAI, were used during the development of Orbit Craft to assist with code generation, debugging, problem-solving, and feature implementation.

AI assistance was used for:

  • Generating and refining HTML, CSS, and JavaScript code.
  • Implementing mission configuration and simulation functionality.
  • Developing engineering calculations and validation logic.
  • Debugging, improving the user interface, and refining existing features.

The project concept, feature direction, design decisions, integration, testing, and final review were guided and carried out by the developer, with AI tools serving as development assistants.

Images and Video: Images used in the website were sourced from external websites and were not AI-generated. The demonstration video is an original screen recording of the application.

Data: Mission references and technical specifications were obtained from external sources and organized for use in the application. AI tools assisted with processing and implementing this information; the underlying reference data was not AI-generated.
